common_name: Miss Frances Crapemyrtle (Deep Red Compact Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container stock in late winter through fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Miss Frances is a Southern Living Plant Collection crapemyrtle selected for deep red summer flowers on a rounded, spreading tree form.

directions: Miss Frances opens deep red flower clusters through summer against lustrous green foliage, carried on a rounded, spreading, multi-trunked tree that shows off grey-orange exfoliating bark once limbed up. It needs little routine pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood in winter, and tolerates drought, clay soil, and the heat of a Gulf South summer once established. Site it with room to spread, since its mature canopy runs wider than many upright crapemyrtle selections. Feed once yearly in spring and deadhead through summer to prolong the bloom season into fall.

common_name: Miss Sandra Crapemyrtle (Purple-Flowered Upright Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container stock in late winter through fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Miss Sandra is a Southern Living Plant Collection crapemyrtle with purple summer flowers on an upright tree form.

directions: Miss Sandra carries purple flower clusters through summer on an upright, narrower frame than many crapemyrtle selections, making it a fit for tighter side-yard or street-tree plantings. It attracts birds and butterflies while in bloom and holds disease resistance and drought tolerance typical of modern crapemyrtle breeding once roots are established. Pruning is optional and best limited to winter removal of dead or crossing branches rather than heavy topping. Feed yearly in spring and water regularly through the first growing season to establish a deep root system.

common_name: Colorama Scarlet Crapemyrtle (Vigorous Scarlet-Flowered Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container stock in late winter through fall in well-drained soil in full sun, setting the root ball 1-2 inches above grade; Colorama Scarlet is a patented, self-branching crapemyrtle bred for scarlet-red summer and fall flowers.

directions: Colorama Scarlet produces scarlet-red flower clusters against deep green deciduous foliage from summer into fall, on a vigorous, self-branching habit that fills in quickly without heavy shaping. It tolerates clay soil and low water once established, and needs only an early-spring shape-up before the first flush of growth rather than seasonal hard pruning. Feed yearly in early spring and apply a shallow mulch ring that stays clear of the trunk. Its wide zone range and birds-and-butterflies appeal make it a reliable summer specimen across much of the Southeast.

common_name: Delta Fusion Crapemyrtle (Dark Pink Dwarf Dark-Foliage Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container stock in late winter through fall in well-drained soil in full sun, setting the root ball 1-2 inches above grade; Delta Fusion is a smaller-statured Delta-series crapemyrtle with dark pink summer flowers.

directions: Delta Fusion stays more compact than most Delta-series crapemyrtles, topping out well under the typical crapemyrtle tree size while still producing dark pink flower clusters through summer. Regular deadheading through the growing season and a fall trim keep the bloom cycle going and the plant tidy. Give it full sun and water on a medium schedule rather than letting it dry out completely between waterings, since its smaller root mass handles drought less readily than full-size selections. Feed yearly in early spring; its compact scale suits accent, hedge, or large container use where a full-size crapemyrtle would overwhelm the space.

common_name: It's a Breeze Red Rose (Dark Red Groundcover Rose)
scientific_name: Rosa hybrid 'Meigremlis' PP25950 (It's a Breeze Red)

planting.note: Plant container roses in spring or fall in a hole twice the pot's width, setting the crown 1-2 inches above grade and mulching lightly; It's a Breeze Red is a patented groundcover rose with dark red repeat blooms.

directions: It's a Breeze Red carries petite, dark red double blooms in clusters of twenty to thirty flowers per stem from spring through fall, on a low, spreading groundcover frame that works as a border, low hedge, or slope planting. It is bred for strong disease resistance and holds up to both winter cold and summer heat across an unusually wide zone range. Feed through the growing season and prune back hard in early spring before new growth to keep the mounded shape dense. Established plants need only moderate water and attract birds and butterflies while in flower.

common_name: It's a Breeze Ivory Blush Rose (White-to-Pink Groundcover Rose)
scientific_name: Rosa hybrid 'Meimeigea' PP26310 (It's a Breeze Ivory Blush)

planting.note: Plant container roses in spring or fall in a hole twice the pot's width, setting the crown 1-2 inches above grade and mulching lightly; It's a Breeze Ivory Blush is a patented groundcover rose with white flowers that blush pale pink in cool weather.

directions: It's a Breeze Ivory Blush opens pure white double flowers that take on a soft pink blush during cool temperatures, repeating from spring through fall on glossy dark green evergreen foliage. Its low, spreading growth habit suits borders, low hedges, mass plantings, and containers where a full-size shrub rose would be too large. It is disease- and pest-resistant with easy care needs, requiring only a balanced feed through the bloom season and an early-spring shape-up before new growth emerges. Water on a medium schedule once established; it tolerates both deep winter cold and summer heat across its broad hardiness range.

common_name: Southgate Brandi Rhododendron (Compact Pink-Flowered Dwarf Rhododendron)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil in part shade to shade; Southgate Brandi is a heat-tolerant dwarf rhododendron bred to perform in Deep South gardens as well as traditional rhododendron climates.

directions: Southgate Brandi opens deep pink buds into ruffled pink flowers each spring on a compact, dwarf evergreen frame bred specifically for heat tolerance beyond what older rhododendron selections can handle. Part shade to shade suits it best, particularly in the hotter end of its range, and it performs equally well in traditional cooler rhododendron country. Feed once yearly in early spring and prune only after the spring bloom finishes, since later cuts remove the next season's flower buds. Medium water and disease- and pest-resistant breeding make it a lower-maintenance option than many classic rhododendron cultivars in accent, hedge, or mass plantings.

common_name: Southgate Divine Rhododendron (White-Flowered Purple-Flecked Dwarf Rhododendron)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil in part shade to shade; Southgate Divine is a heat-tolerant dwarf rhododendron with light pink buds opening to white, purple-flecked flowers.

directions: Southgate Divine opens from light pink buds into white spring flowers flecked with purple, a distinctive bicolor effect among the Southgate rhododendron line. Its compact habit and heat tolerance let it thrive in Deep South gardens where older rhododendron cultivars struggle with summer heat, while performing just as well in cooler, traditional rhododendron regions. Plant in part shade to shade in acidic, well-drained soil, and prune only right after spring flowering to avoid cutting off next year's buds. Feed yearly in early spring and keep watering consistent through the first year to establish roots before easing to a medium schedule.

common_name: Southgate Splendor Rhododendron (Medium Pink Dwarf Rhododendron)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil in part shade to shade; Southgate Splendor is a patented, heat-tolerant dwarf rhododendron with medium pink spring flowers.

directions: Southgate Splendor carries medium pink spring flowers on a dense, dwarf evergreen frame bred for compact habit and winter and fall foliage interest beyond the bloom season. Like the rest of the Southgate line it tolerates Deep South summer heat better than older rhododendron selections while still performing in traditional cooler rhododendron climates. Plant in part shade to shade in acidic, well-drained soil, and prune only immediately after spring bloom to preserve next year's flower buds. Feed once yearly in early spring; medium water and disease- and pest-resistant breeding make it a practical choice for accent, hedge, or mass planting.

common_name: Golden Oakland Holly (Golden Variegated Oak-Leaf Holly)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Golden Oakland is a patented holly selected for golden-variegated, oak-shaped evergreen foliage.

directions: Golden Oakland stands out among hollies for its oak-shaped leaves edged in golden-yellow variegation, giving year-round color on an upright evergreen tree that needs minimal pruning to hold its form. It works well as a privacy hedge, specimen accent, or large container planting where its foliage color can be appreciated up close. The plant is deer resistant and draws birds and butterflies, with medium water needs once established. Feed yearly in early spring and prune in early spring before new growth begins if any shaping is wanted.
